framework: National Curriculum in England (2014): English programmes of study, Key Stages 1 to 3, with EYFS Literacy and Communication and Language for Reception
statusNote: All content was compared with the official text, read as raw text from the gov.uk and assets.publishing.service.gov.uk PDFs listed in sources: the primary (KS1-2) and secondary (KS3) English programmes of study, Appendix 1 (spelling), Appendix 2 (vocabulary, grammar and punctuation), the glossary (used to check terminology) and the EYFS statutory framework for group and school-based providers (dated 13 July 2026, effective 1 September 2026): the Communication and Language, Literacy and Fine Motor sections and Early Learning Goals. EYFS assessment and welfare sections were not needed for this syllabus. The statutory content is set by key stage (Year 1 and Year 2 individually in KS1; two-year blocks in KS2; KS3 as one block); the year-by-year allocation, the phonics order in Reception and Year 1, and the chosen texts (The Explorer, war poetry, Of Mice and Men, and similar) are the school's recommended sequence, not statutory. Spelling and grammar are recorded at topic level in paraphrase; the Year 3-4 and Year 5-6 statutory word lists are named, not reproduced. Year 1 was rebuilt in November 2026 to the TGA Year 1 Curriculum Pack: one unit per half term, following Tarbiyyah Primary's Cornerstones projects (2026-27 order), White Rose maths and Little Wandle phonics.

purpose: English is essential to education: pupils must speak, read and write fluently to take part in society.
Reading, especially literature, supports cultural, emotional, intellectual, social and spiritual development.
Pupils should write clearly for different audiences, and use discussion to learn and explain ideas.
Pupils build a wide vocabulary, understand grammar and conventions, and appreciate the literary heritage.

keyStages.years: Reception (EYFS framework in force from 1 September 2026)

statements: ELG Listening, Attention and Understanding: listen attentively and respond with relevant questions, comments and actions.
Comment on what they have heard and ask questions to clarify understanding.
Hold back-and-forth conversation with teachers and peers.
ELG Speaking: join group, class and one-to-one discussion, offering ideas with recently taught vocabulary.
Offer explanations for why things might happen, using new vocabulary from stories, non-fiction, rhymes and poems.
Express ideas and feelings in full sentences, using past, present and future tenses and conjunctions, with support.
ELG Comprehension: retell stories and narratives in their own words, using recently introduced vocabulary.
Anticipate key events in stories where appropriate.
Use and understand new vocabulary in discussion of stories, non-fiction, rhymes, poems and role play.
ELG Word Reading: say a sound for each letter of the alphabet and at least 10 digraphs.
Read words consistent with their phonic knowledge by sound-blending.
Read aloud simple sentences and books matched to phonics, including some common exception words.
ELG Writing: write recognisable letters, most of them correctly formed.
Spell words by identifying sounds and representing them with a letter or letters.
Write simple phrases and sentences that others can read.
Related ELG Fine Motor Skills: hold a pencil effectively, using the tripod grip in almost all cases.
Listen and respond to adults and peers; ask relevant questions.
Build vocabulary and articulate and justify answers and opinions.
Give structured descriptions, explanations and narratives.
Take part in collaborative conversation, staying on topic and building on comments.
Use spoken language to speculate, hypothesise and explore ideas.
Speak audibly and fluently in Standard English; take part in drama, presentations and debate.
Consider different viewpoints and select registers for different purposes.
Blend unfamiliar words using known grapheme-phoneme correspondences, including alternative sounds.
Read common exception words and notice unusual spelling-sound links (Year 1).
Read decodable books aloud accurately and reread them for fluency.
In Year 2, read most words without sounding out, and split longer words into syllables.
Listen to and discuss stories, poems and non-fiction above independent reading level.
Retell familiar stories; recite poems by heart; discuss word meanings.
Discuss the sequence of events and how information is related (Year 2); recognise recurring literary language.
Make inferences, ask and answer questions and predict.
Year 2 guidance (non-statutory): learn about cause and effect in narrative and non-fiction.
Explain clearly their understanding of what is read and heard.
Spell taught phonemes, common exception words and days of the week (Year 1).
Spell with alternative graphemes, homophones, contractions and the singular possessive apostrophe (Year 2).
Add suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less and -ly (Year 2).
Form lower-case letters, capitals and digits correctly; begin joining strokes in Year 2.
Say sentences aloud, compose them orally, then write and reread them.
Sequence sentences into short narratives (Year 1).
Write personal, fictional and real narratives, accounts and poetry (Year 2).
Plan with key vocabulary; proofread for sense and consistent tense.
Use capital letters, full stops, question and exclamation marks.
Join words and clauses using 'and' (Year 1); use subordination and co-ordination (Year 2).
Use statements, questions, exclamations and commands; expanded noun phrases.
Use commas in lists and apostrophes for contractions and singular possession.

keyStages.years: Year 3 to Year 6 (lower: Years 3 to 4; upper: Years 5 to 6)

statements: Use root words, prefixes and suffixes (morphology and etymology) to read and understand new words.
Read further exception words and check unfamiliar pronunciations.
By Year 5, read most words effortlessly and attend to every letter.
Read widely: fiction, poetry, plays, non-fiction, myths and legends, classic and modern texts.
Explain words in context, infer feelings and motives with evidence, and predict.
Summarise ideas across paragraphs; identify how language, structure and presentation shape meaning.
Distinguish fact from opinion; evaluate figurative language (upper KS2).
Prepare and perform poems and plays; learn poetry by heart.
Discuss and challenge views courteously; compare characters, settings and texts.
Spell using prefixes, suffixes, homophones, silent letters and commonly misspelt words.
Use the possessive apostrophe with plural nouns; check spellings in a dictionary.
Write legibly in a joined style, faster and more fluently by Year 6; choose the right implement.
Plan by identifying audience and purpose, using models and research.
Draft with paragraphs, settings, characters, dialogue and organisational devices such as headings.
Evaluate and edit own and others' writing; keep tense consistent; proofread.
Perform compositions with suitable intonation, volume and movement.
Use a wider range of conjunctions, fronted adverbials with commas, and the present perfect (Years 3 to 4).
Punctuate direct speech; use Standard English verb forms instead of local spoken forms (Year 4 appendix).
Use relative clauses, modal verbs, passive verbs and expanded noun phrases (Years 5 to 6).
Use brackets, dashes, colons, semi-colons and hyphens accurately (Years 5 to 6).
Recognise formal and informal structures, including the subjunctive.
Read widely: whole books, short stories, poems and plays from different periods and authors.
Include pre-1914 and contemporary literature, two Shakespeare plays and seminal world literature.
Study at least two authors in depth each year.
Make inferences with evidence; consider purpose, audience and context.
Analyse how language, grammar, structure and organisation create meaning.
Recognise poetic conventions; understand how drama works in performance; compare texts critically.
Write accurately, fluently and at length for many purposes and audiences.
Forms include essays, narratives, scripts, poetry, talks, arguments and letters.
Summarise and organise material; support ideas with factual detail.
Use rhetorical and literary devices from reading.
Plan, draft, edit and proofread; improve coherence.
Extend Appendix 2 knowledge to analyse challenging texts and the effect of grammar.
Use new vocabulary and constructions consciously in writing and speech.
Understand differences between spoken and written language and between registers.
Use Standard English confidently; use linguistic and literary terminology precisely.
Use Standard English in formal and informal contexts, including classroom discussion.
Give short speeches and presentations; take part in formal debates.
Summarise and build on others' points in structured discussion.
Improvise, rehearse and perform scripts and poetry, using role, tone, volume and stillness.

keyStages.years: Years 1 to 6 (applied and extended at KS3)

statements: Year 1 (revising Reception): alphabet sounds, digraphs, segmenting words into sounds, adjacent consonants.
Year 1: ff, ll, ss, zz, ck after short vowels; n before k; syllables; tch; /v/ followed by e.
Year 1: adding -s/-es, and -ing, -ed, -er, -est where the root word does not change.
Year 1: vowel digraphs and trigraphs, such as ai, oy, ee, ea, oo, ow, igh, air.
Year 1: words ending -y; ph and wh; k for /k/; prefix un-; compound words; common exception words.
Year 2: /dʒ/ spelt ge, dge or g; c before e, i, y; kn, gn and wr at word starts.
Year 2: word endings -le, -el, -al, -il, and -y for /aɪ/ (cry, fly).
Year 2: adding -es, -ed, -er, -est to words ending -y; dropping e before -ing; doubling consonants.
Year 2: a after w and qu; or and ar after w; /ʒ/ spelt s; -ey.
Year 2: suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly; contractions; singular possessive apostrophe; -tion.
Year 2: homophones and near-homophones; further common exception words (such as door, because, great, people).
Years 3-4: doubling the final consonant before vowel suffixes in multi-syllable words, depending on stress.
Years 3-4: y spelt for /ɪ/ (gym, myth) and ou for /ʌ/ (young, touch).
Years 3-4: prefixes dis-, mis-, in- (il-, im-, ir-), re-, sub-, inter-, super-, anti-, auto-.
Years 3-4: suffixes -ation, -ly (with its exceptions), -ous, and endings -sure, -ture, -sion.
Years 3-4: endings for /ʃən/ spelt -tion, -sion, -ssion, -cian, chosen by the root word.
Years 3-4: ch for /k/ and /ʃ/; -gue and -que; sc for /s/; ei, eigh, ey for /eɪ/.
Years 3-4: possessive apostrophe with plural words; more homophones; statutory list of 100 words.
Years 5-6: endings -cious, -tious, -cial, -tial; -ant/-ance/-ancy and -ent/-ence/-ency.
Years 5-6: endings -able, -ible, -ably, -ibly; adding suffixes to words ending -fer.
Years 5-6: the hyphen after prefixes; ei after c; the letter string ough; silent letters.
Years 5-6: homophones and words often confused (advice/advise, affect/effect, principal/principle).
Years 5-6: statutory list of 100 words, with morphology and etymology as clues to spelling.
Year 1: plural -s/-es; verb suffixes without spelling change; prefix un-; joining with and.
Year 1: sequencing sentences into short narratives; finger spaces; capital letters, full stops, question and exclamation marks.
Year 1 terms: letter, capital letter, word, singular, plural, sentence, punctuation, full stop, question mark, exclamation mark.
Year 2: nouns from -ness, -er and compounding; adjectives from -ful, -less; -er, -est and -ly.
Year 2: subordination (when, if, that, because), co-ordination (or, and, but), expanded noun phrases.
Year 2: statement, question, exclamation and command forms; consistent past and present tense, including progressive.
Year 2: commas in lists; apostrophes for missing letters and singular possession.
Year 2 terms: noun, noun phrase, compound, suffix, adjective, adverb, verb, tense, apostrophe, comma.
Year 3: prefixes forming nouns; a or an; word families; time, place and cause with conjunctions, adverbs, prepositions.
Year 3: paragraphs; headings and sub-headings; present perfect; inverted commas for direct speech.
Year 3 terms: preposition, conjunction, word family, prefix, clause, subordinate clause, direct speech, vowel, consonant, inverted commas.
Year 4: plural versus possessive -s; Standard English verb forms instead of local forms (we were, I did).
Year 4: noun phrases expanded with adjectives, nouns and prepositional phrases; fronted adverbials with commas.
Year 4: paragraphs around a theme; pronoun or noun choice for cohesion; speech punctuation; plural possession.
Year 4 terms: determiner, pronoun, possessive pronoun, adverbial.
Year 5: verbs formed with -ate, -ise, -ify; verb prefixes dis-, de-, mis-, over-, re-.
Year 5: relative clauses; possibility shown by adverbs or modal verbs; cohesion within and across paragraphs.
Year 5: brackets, dashes or commas for parenthesis; commas to clarify meaning.
Year 5 terms: modal verb, relative pronoun, relative clause, parenthesis, bracket, dash, cohesion, ambiguity.
Year 6: formal versus informal vocabulary and structures; synonyms and antonyms; the passive; subjunctive forms.
Year 6: wider cohesive devices including repetition and ellipsis; layout devices for structuring text.
Year 6: semi-colon, colon and dash between clauses; colons and semi-colons in lists; bullet points; hyphens.
Year 6 terms: subject, object, active, passive, synonym, antonym, ellipsis, hyphen, colon, semi-colon, bullet points.

toKS4: KS3 reading, writing, grammar and spoken English prepare pupils for AQA GCSE English Language 8700 and English Literature 8702. For Language, Paper 1 (Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing: AO1, AO2, AO4 reading; AO5, AO6 writing) and Paper 2 (Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives: AO1, AO2, AO3 reading; AO5, AO6 writing) each carry 80 marks and 50%; the Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9) is reported separately. For Literature, Paper 1 (Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel: 64 marks, 40%) and Paper 2 (Modern texts and poetry: 96 marks, 60%) assess AO1 to AO4. KS3 inference and evidence feed AO1, language and structure analysis feeds AO2, comparison of poems and viewpoints feeds AO3 (Language) and Literature's poetry comparison, context feeds Literature AO3, and the writing and grammar thread feeds AO5, AO6 and Literature AO4. The KS3 requirement for two Shakespeare plays and pre-1914 literature leads to the Paper 1 set texts.
